w: Dr. Matthew Litz gave this session in two parts. He recorded the antibiotics half ("I give this lecture every year to the dental students"; the file posted is dated March 2024), then taught host modulation in class on Nov 5, after a short recap of the antibiotics. The antibiotics notes come from the recording, the slides and that recap; the host modulation section comes from the class. He boiled the lecture down to "the most basic information that I feel like you need when you start treating patients in the clinic." Bacteria cause it, but antibiotics are only for select cases Periodontal disease is initiated by a relatively specific group of indigenous oral bacteria: predominantly gram-negative anaerobic rods in a biofilm. "Anytime anybody ever asks you, what causes periodontal disease? The answer is bacteria and plaque. You find that answer on your multiple choice test question and you circle it." In class he put it more bluntly: "Don't even look at the other answers because they're wrong." Smoking and diabetes can compound it, but without bacteria there is no attachment or bone loss. Because it is a bacterial infection, antibiotics are justified, but only in selected cases. Perio treatment, like restorative treatment, has phases. Phase I is non-surgical: oral hygiene instructions first (30-45 minutes in his office, and "arguably the most important appointment that the patient will have," because nothing works long-term if the patient can't keep their teeth clean), then scaling and root planing, then, if needed, chemotherapeutic agents, chemical substances that provide a clinical therapeutic benefit (Carranza). Antibiotics fall here: if used at all, they are used in Phase I after scaling and root planing. When to consider antibiotics: an acute periodontal infection with systemic manifestations (fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy: a localized infection starting to spread); aggressive periodontitis, which hits young patients with severe attachment and bone loss in a short time and has to be treated aggressively; and refractory periodontitis, where a patient who has done everything asked (good home care, thorough SRP, surgery, 3-month maintenance) still loses attachment. And always as an adjunct to surgical and non-surgical therapy: "the use of systemic or locally delivered antibiotics is not to be used as a monotherapy in the treatment of periodontal disease." That was his main take-home message. Why antibiotics alone don't work: biofilms The putative pathogens live in a biofilm, an aggregation of multiple microorganisms: if one microbial colony is a house, a biofilm is a subdivision in a protective bubble. Biofilms are a trait of supragingival and subgingival plaque. They protect and harbor the resident bacteria, let colonies survive harsh environments, and are insoluble, which makes them hard to remove: rinsing, water irrigation and mouthwashes leave them in place, like a dirty pot left soaking overnight that still has to be scrubbed. That is mechanical debridement: the patient's toothbrush and floss, and our curettes and ultrasonics. Some biofilm organisms survive antibiotic concentrations 500-1000 times greater than systemic delivery can reach. In class he called this the point to "star" and "know for life": the only way to get rid of a biofilm is mechanical debridement. A mouthrinse can supplement it, never replace it. Biofilms make bacteria resistant to antibiotics in three ways: (1) a physical barrier that makes antibiotic penetration difficult; (2) an increased concentration of beta-lactamase inside, which destroys the beta-lactam ring of our strongest antibiotics ("anytime you see -ase on the end of a word, that's what it destroys"); and (3) a slower growth rate of the resident bacteria, which makes them less susceptible to many antibiotics. A systemic antibiotic enters the bloodstream and spreads evenly from head to toe ("it's not a heat-seeking missile"), then diffuses into the periodontal connective tissue, junctional epithelium and crevicular region and into the gingival crevicular fluid. But the concentration there is inadequate to kill the organisms in a biofilm without mechanical debridement. Debride first, then add the antibiotic. Bactericidal or bacteriostatic Bacteriostatic agents inhibit the growth and reproduction of bacteria without killing them, so the body can finish the job. Bactericidal agents kill bacteria directly, but only bacteria that are actively dividing, a narrow window. That is why a biofilm's slower growth hurts our strongest antibiotics. It is also why, when two antibiotics are given at the same time, they must be both bactericidal or both bacteriostatic, never one of each: the bacteriostatic drug slows growth and shuts the bactericidal drug's only window. Antibiotics are classified by molecular structure and mechanism: they interrupt the synthesis of structural components or alter metabolic functions unique to microbial cells. Amoxicillin, and how to write a prescription Amoxicillin: a semisynthetic penicillin effective against gram-negative and gram-positive organisms; bactericidal by inhibiting cell wall synthesis; extended spectrum, covering many periodontal pathogens; useful in localized and generalized aggressive periodontitis. It contains a beta-lactam ring, so beta-lactamase-producing bacteria (including many periodontal pathogens) can inactivate it. Dose: 500 mg, one po tid for 7 days. Some write 875 mg bid: fewer doses a day, better compliance, and a drug only works if the patient takes it. Abbreviations: po = by mouth; qd = once a day; bid = twice; tid = three times; qid = four times. A prescription must include the medication and strength (amoxicillin 500 mg), the quantity or volume to dispense (21 tablets for one tid for 7 days), and the instructions for use (Sig: 1 tab po tid). Also the patient's name, date of birth and address, the date, your name, address and phone number, refills, and your signature. Hypersensitivity is the most common side effect; about 10-15% of adults are reported to have an allergic response to penicillin. Before handing over any prescription, get verbal confirmation that the patient isn't allergic to it. When a patient reports an allergy, ask what reaction they have. An upset stomach is a side effect, not an allergy. Hives or difficulty breathing (the throat closing) point to a true, potentially fatal anaphylactic reaction: then don't give that drug or anything in its class. Many organisms are now resistant to amoxicillin. Like nearly every antibiotic, it can interfere with oral contraceptives and has shown increased bleeding times in patients on Coumadin (warfarin). Antibiotics can reduce the gut flora that make vitamin K, warfarin's antagonist, so less warfarin is inactivated and its level rises. That doesn't mean you can't prescribe; it means you let the physician know and the physician decides whether to adjust. Never change a medication another clinician prescribed. Augmentin and the cephalosporins Augmentin combines amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, a beta-lactamase inhibitor: it "inactivates their inactivator," so the amoxicillin can work. Effective against gram-positive and more gram-negative organisms, including anaerobes; useful in aggressive or refractory periodontitis. It may cause more GI upset (so give it with food) and is significantly more expensive than other penicillins. Written as 500 or 875 mg (the amoxicillin dose); the clavulanic acid stays 125 mg either way. Cephalosporins: beta-lactam compounds similar in structure and action to the penicillins; bactericidal by inhibiting cell wall synthesis. Grouped in generations (1st to 4th on the slide; a 5th exists) by spectrum and order of development: later generations move from mostly gram-positive toward gram-negative coverage and more resistance to beta-lactamase, so perio favors the later ones. Some evidence of increased bone penetration; may be given with food. About 10% cross-reactivity in patients allergic to penicillin: don't give one to a patient allergic to penicillin who is unsure about cephalosporins. As taught, a patient allergic to cephalosporins has a 100% chance of penicillin allergy, so move on to another class. Cephalosporins can also interfere with oral contraceptives and increase bleeding time with warfarin. Clindamycin A derivative of lincomycin. It reversibly binds the 50S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting protein synthesis; usually bactericidal, bacteriostatic depending on drug concentration, infection site and organism. Effective against a wide range of periodontal bacteria and the usual first choice for a patient with a true allergy to penicillins and cephalosporins. Dose: 150-300 mg po tid for 7 days. Its known side effect is pseudomembranous colitis: altered gut flora let Clostridium difficile (C. diff) overgrow, which can be fatal. The condition is reported with other antibiotics too, but clindamycin "gets a bad rap" for it. Avoid it in patients with a history of colitis. Tetracyclines Tetracycline is a broad-spectrum bacteriostatic antibiotic that reversibly binds the 30S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting protein synthesis; it covers gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, aerobes and anaerobes. But widespread use over decades has bred resistant strains, so its efficacy for oral infections is significantly less than the penicillins'. It may be indicated where Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans is the prominent pathogen (localized aggressive periodontitis). As a bacteriostatic drug it may negate bactericidal agents that only work on growing cells. Adverse effects: GI upset is the most common (nausea, vomiting, sore mouth, diarrhea, abdominal distention), and a patient who feels that bad stops taking it. Prolonged clotting time (less vitamin K from gut flora). It is deposited in bone and teeth during calcification: intrinsic stain and enamel hypoplasia (pitting, cusp deformities, more caries), so avoid it in pregnancy and in children under 8. Photosensitivity: tell patients to avoid direct sun. Absorption is inhibited by divalent and trivalent cations (calcium, magnesium, iron, aluminum): no milk or dairy, iron vitamins, mineral supplements or antacids, and take it 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals. The semisynthetic derivatives doxycycline (Vibramycin) and minocycline (Minocin) are absorbed more completely and disturb the gut flora less, so they cause less GI upset. Doxycycline 100 mg po once a day; minocycline 100 mg po bid. Doxycycline is also given at a sub-antimicrobial 20 mg bid for its anticollagenase effect (Periostat, below). Macrolides Erythromycin, azithromycin and clarithromycin bind the 50S subunit (like clindamycin), inhibit protein synthesis in gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, and are bacteriostatic and generally narrow spectrum. Azithromycin and clarithromycin are more active against anaerobes than erythromycin. Erythromycin: aerobic gram-positive and some anaerobic coverage, but a high incidence of bacterial resistance, so it is not recommended for periodontal disease, and nearly everyone taking it gets some GI upset. Allergy is rare, but avoid it in patients allergic to another macrolide. 250-500 mg po q6h (qid). Azithromycin, the Z-Pak: 500 mg the first day, then 250 mg on days 2-5, five days in all, easy to comply with. Food significantly decreases its absorption: give it 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals. Clarithromycin (Biaxin): well absorbed with or without food. It has caused fetal abnormalities in animals and is pregnancy category C: avoid it in pregnant women. 250-500 mg po q12h (bid). ("If there's ever an award for the best smelling antibiotic, this wins": vanilla.) Macrolide interactions: they can raise plasma levels of, and potentiate, many drugs, including digoxin (risking digoxin toxicity), Dilantin, oral anticoagulants (warfarin), cyclosporine, midazolam, corticosteroids and theophylline. Digoxin, a positive inotrope for heart failure, has a narrow therapeutic range. His story: Van Gogh, given digoxin in an asylum, painted The Starry Night's halos around bright lights, a symptom of digoxin toxicity. Metronidazole Effective only against obligate anaerobes, particularly spirochetes. It reacts with bacterial DNA, inhibiting DNA replication, and is almost always bactericidal. Useful in aggressive periodontitis and ANUG (acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis). Often combined with amoxicillin to widen the spectrum, with highly effective results: both are bactericidal, so they can be given together. 250 mg tid. Food delays but doesn't reduce absorption; bacterial resistance is low. Cautions: it increases the anticoagulant effect of warfarin (check with the physician); it may decrease the renal excretion of lithium; it is teratogenic, so avoid it in pregnancy. Tell every patient two things: their urine may turn orange-red, and alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction with an extreme headache, like Antabuse. No alcohol. Ciprofloxacin A fluoroquinolone that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase; bactericidal and extended spectrum. Effective against gram-negative bacteria, but anaerobes are largely resistant, and anaerobes drive periodontal attachment loss. It is most rapidly absorbed when taken 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals. It may impede the metabolism of theophylline, caffeine and warfarin, and may cause a phototoxic reaction (avoid excessive sun). 500 mg po bid, alone or with metronidazole (which covers the anaerobes) for localized aggressive periodontitis. In practice it comes far down the list: after penicillins, cephalosporins, clindamycin (ruled out by colitis) and a Z-Pak that didn't sit well. The dosing chart: "I would know this for the exam" Asked about doses in class, he said, "I definitely would know dosing. Absolutely," and pointed to the chart at the end of his slides: "I would know this. I would know this for the exam. It's important to know." The usual adult dose and length of treatment for each regimen on it: Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (Augmentin): 250 or 500 mg tid for 10 days. Amoxicillin plus metronidazole: 375 mg amoxicillin tid plus 250 mg metronidazole tid, for 7 days. Clindamycin: 150-300 mg qid for 10 days. Doxycycline: 100 mg bid the first day, then 100 mg a day (once, or 50 mg bid), for 10-14 days. Metronidazole: 250 mg tid or qid for 10 days. Minocycline: 200 mg bid the first day, then 100 mg bid, for 10-14 days. Tetracycline: 250 mg qid for 14-21 days, the longest course on the chart. The two regimens with metronidazole are not recommended for children under 16, and the tetracyclines are dosed for children only over age 8. A few doses differ from the drug-by-drug slides, so know both: the clindamycin slide gives 150-300 mg tid for 7 days, the doxycycline slide 100 mg once a day, and Augmentin is usually written as 500 or 875 mg. Complications of systemic antibiotics Alteration of the GI flora with GI disturbances (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea); overgrowth of opportunistic bacteria such as C. diff; decreased effectiveness of oral contraceptives; and increased bleeding time with oral anticoagulants. To help avoid them: prophylactic Lactobacillus acidophilus (yogurt or buttermilk with active cultures) and antifungal therapy (nystatin, or Diflucan 150 mg, one tablet at the start of the course, for patients prone to yeast infections). Local drug delivery Locally delivered antimicrobials are an adjunct to scaling and root planing, placed subgingivally at the completion of SRP, after the biofilm is disrupted. An effective agent delivers high concentrations sustained over a long time, applied directly to the infected site, which decreases or eliminates the potential for antibiotic resistance. The disadvantage, local or systemic: neither can alter the anatomical deformities (the irregular bone) left by the disease. They are not effective against tissue-invasive organisms. Indications: localized sites that don't respond to Phase I (the textbook answer, "not a great indication"; generalized residual pockets need surgery, not a dozen expensive cartridges) and, the real indication, localized sites in an otherwise stable maintenance patient: one site that was 3 mm for years is now 5 mm and bleeding, a last attempt before surgery. Anesthetize, debride with the ultrasonic and hand instruments, then place the agent, and re-evaluate in 4-6 weeks. Not a replacement for conventional therapy, and not for aggressive periodontitis. The three agents sold in the US: PerioChip: 2.5 mg chlorhexidine in a gelatin matrix, 4 x 5 x 0.35 mm ("you don't need to know these dimensions"). Self-retentive on contact with moisture, inserted into the pocket at the end of SRP, biodegradable (no removal appointment). Release peaks about 2 hours after placement, then decreases over about 9 days. Atridox: 10% doxycycline in a biodegradable polymer, in two syringes: A holds 450 mg of the Atrigel delivery system, B holds 42.5 mg of doxycycline. Couple them and mix back and forth about 1½ minutes (100 cycles). Applied into the pocket, the excess packed in with a cord-packing instrument; it hardens, then dissolves over 3-4 weeks (no removal). The patient avoids brushing, flossing and eating at the site for at least 7 days. Arestin: 1 mg minocycline microspheres in a biodegradable polymer, in unit-dose cartridges on a handle. Bioadhesive on contact with moisture. Insert the plastic tip to the base of the pocket and inject slowly while withdrawing. No removal appointment; the minocycline keeps a therapeutic concentration for 14 days. The patient avoids brushing the site for 12 hours and flossing it for 10 days. He still uses it in his practice from time to time. Host modulation: what it means Dr. Litz taught this part in class. He started by taking the term apart. A host is "an organism from which a parasite obtains its nourishment": in periodontal disease, the patient who harbors the plaque. Modulation is "an alteration of function or status of something in response to a stimulus or an altered chemical or physical environment" (Taber's). So the question is: can we change the way a patient responds to the periodontal pathogens, the response that leads to attachment loss? It is taught with antibiotics because host modulation turned to drugs, antibiotics among them. Bacteria are the key; the host response is the engine "This is a really, really important slide." Gram-negative bacteria are required for periodontal disease to start and progress: they are the primary etiologic factor. But they are not sufficient to cause the clinical signs of attachment loss. "Know this last bullet point": it is ultimately the host response to the bacteria that mediates tissue destruction (Reddy 2003). It is largely the way our bodies fight the bacteria that makes the deep pockets and the bone loss on radiographs. He admitted that as a student he could repeat this on an exam but only understood it as a resident. His flowchart reads left to right, like a sentence. It always begins with the microbial challenge. Once plaque builds up along the gingival margin, the body recognizes it as foreign and mounts a host immune-inflammatory response, sending cells to destroy the bacteria, as it should. But the site turns into a war zone with collateral damage: while fighting the bacteria, our cells release pro-inflammatory cytokines and prostaglandins, which drive connective tissue and bone breakdown, seen as the clinical signs of disease: deeper pockets and bone loss. A deeper pocket is a niche for more bacteria; a bigger bacterial load calls for a bigger cellular response and more cytokines, which means more breakdown: a vicious cycle. The take-home: it always begins with bacteria. Periodontal disease is not an autoimmune disease; the body doesn't destroy itself without a stimulus. His analogy is the car in your garage. The engine (the host response) is what gets you from periodontal health to periodontal disease, but at two in the morning it won't start by itself. It sits there dormant until someone turns the key, and the key is the bacteria. At the cellular level "You know these next two slides, you're going to have a pretty good understanding of the way periodontal disease works." How bacteria build up: a salivary pellicle forms within minutes of a prophylaxis and is the foundation that promotes bacterial adhesion (by the time the patient pays at the front desk, the foundation is laid). The first colonizers are mostly gram-positive cocci, fed by dietary proteins in saliva. As hygiene slips, plaque along the gingival margin inflames the soft tissue, which creates the environment for the late colonizers, the orange and then the red complexes, fed by blood and GCF. Colonization is sequential, not haphazard. The bacteria live in a biofilm, which protects them and works as a simple circulatory system, bringing nutrients and removing wastes. How the body fights back: the cascade starts with complement, a cluster of serum proteins whose primary function is to control inflammation. Complement can lyse bacterial cell membranes directly, but its main job is as a chemoattractant for phagocytes (PMNs). It also releases histamine from mast cells, which increases vascular permeability: fluid and cells leak into the tissue, and that is the edema of inflammation. Neutrophils (PMNs) are the first responders, like the paramedics at a wreck: they arrive within about 24-48 hours of a bacterial insult to remove foreign agents. If they can't keep up, macrophages arrive later. Both are good cells ("if you didn't have them, you'd be dead"), but both release cytokines, intercellular signals that regulate cellular activity, including immune function. His one example of a cytokine is IL-1, also called osteoclast activating factor. It activates osteoclasts (bone breakdown: a "blast" builds, a "clast" destroys), stimulates collagenase (collagen breakdown: "-ase" breaks down what it's attached to) and activates PGE2. All of this releases MMPs (matrix metalloproteinases) and more PGE2, and connective tissue and bone are lost: "kind of sounds a lot like periodontal disease." Bacteria can make enzymes that break down periodontal structures directly, but the progression and severity of attachment loss is primarily mediated by the host's immune cells. The host response is perhaps the single most important determinant of disease severity, progression and even response to therapy: host-derived enzymes (MMPs) and osteoclasts upregulated by cytokines cause most of the destruction. Bacteria are essential for periodontitis but insufficient by themselves to cause it. Host modulation therapy, and why to step lightly Phase I therapy targets one part of the process: removing plaque reduces the bacterial load that drives the host's inflammatory response. But bacteria are never completely eliminated by scaling and root planing, especially as pockets get deeper and in furcations. Host modulation therapy (HMT) asks whether we can down-regulate the destructive aspects and up-regulate the protective aspects of the host response so that, with conventional therapy such as SRP, the balance tips toward health. Why isn't it further along, when the cellular picture has been known for years? His caution: "You better know what you're doing before you start monkeying around with this." Turn someone's host response down too far and a seemingly innocent bacterial infection could turn serious, even lethal. "This is territory that we really, really need to step lightly." Host modulation isn't new to medicine, which uses it for chronic progressive disorders such as arthritis and osteoporosis. It is fairly new in dentistry: introduced in the 1990s (Williams and Golub, 1990), when pharmacologic agents, antibiotics among them, were found to possibly slow periodontitis. That is why it rides along with the antibiotics lecture. NSAIDs NSAIDs such as aspirin and ibuprofen inhibit the formation of prostaglandins, including PGE2, which neutrophils, macrophages, fibroblasts and gingival epithelial cells make in response to bacteria. PGE2 upregulates osteoclasts and bone resorption, so blocking it is a "pretty good first step." Given daily for up to 3 years, NSAIDs slowed alveolar bone destruction, but daily dosing is necessary: one dose, or a week or two, does nothing. That is the problem, because prolonged NSAID use causes GI problems (a bad gastric ulcer can do serious damage), hemorrhage from decreased platelet aggregation, and renal or hepatic impairment. "We can't just blindly start prescribing NSAIDs" to every periodontal patient, so long-term NSAID use for host modulation hasn't developed. Bisphosphonates Bisphosphonates are not new drugs. They are bone-seeking agents that inhibit bone resorption by inhibiting osteoclasts, may have anticollagenase effects too, and some studies show changes in white blood cell counts. At first glance, "we just found the magic bullet." The catch is bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (BRONJ): bone necrosis after an invasive dental procedure (a simple extraction or periodontal surgery counts), with some reports of it happening spontaneously. These drugs are common, given mostly to older women for osteoporosis, by mouth or in high-dose IV forms, and most complications are with the high-dose IV forms. BRONJ is not an infection, though it can look like one: the gingiva dies back and exposes bone that becomes necrotic. Dead bone can't come back, and left exposed it will get infected, so an oral surgeon has to scrape it off. But scraping is trauma, and trauma is what causes BRONJ: a lesion the size of a dime can come back the size of a quarter or a half dollar, a vicious cycle that is very hard to treat. Stopping the drug doesn't help quickly: bisphosphonates have a very long half-life and stay in the system for years. BRONJ has largely stunted bisphosphonates as host modulation therapy: no bisphosphonate is approved for periodontal disease. Periostat (sub-antimicrobial dose doxycycline) Periostat is the first FDA-approved systemic (by mouth) drug for host modulation, used as an adjunct to scaling and root planing: the same rules apply, and the biofilm still has to be disrupted mechanically. It is a low, sub-antimicrobial dose of doxycycline (SDD). Doxycycline as an antibiotic is 100 mg once a day; Periostat is 20 mg twice a day (bid), a fifth of the dose. At that dose it has no antimicrobial activity (the bacteria take one look at it and leave it alone), so resistance is not evident and it can be given long-term. Its mechanism is to inhibit collagenase, particularly the collagenase made by the host's own cells such as PMNs, where most of the destruction happens. Take it 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal and avoid calcium-containing products. It is contraindicated with hypersensitivity to doxycycline or other tetracyclines, in pregnant or lactating women, and in children under 12. Does it work? Many studies say yes. His example is Caton et al., 2000, a randomized, multicenter, double-blind trial. Both groups had periodontitis and got the same SRP; one then took a placebo, the other Periostat 20 mg bid, for nine months, with re-evaluations at 3, 6 and 9 months. The Periostat group had statistically significant extra pocket reduction at every visit (4-6 mm pockets: 0.95 mm with Periostat vs 0.69 mm with placebo at 9 months; 7 mm or deeper: 1.68 vs 1.2 mm) and the same pattern in attachment gain (1.03 vs 0.86 mm; 1.35 vs 1.17 mm). He said not to learn this study's numbers, just what it shows: statistically significant, but is it clinically significant? These are fractions of a millimeter. It helps where we need all the help we can get, in refractory and aggressive periodontitis. Efficacy beyond 9 months and safety beyond 12 months haven't been established, and the net changes were limited. The AAP: adjunctive therapies (systemic antibiotics, local antibiotics, Periostat) are not a substitute for mechanical debridement, meticulous home care and the other therapies that reduce the bacterial load. In summary, controlling the bacteria remains the primary focus: the dirty pot still has to be scrubbed. Host modulation can be considered for patients with risk factors that can't be modified or aren't easily modified, such as smoking and diabetes. Compliance is mandatory: the pill is taken twice a day, and patients must hear that it replaces neither exceptional home care and plaque control nor their frequent maintenance visits. As with blood pressure or diabetes medicine, patients tend to think a pill cures everything; it helps, but it is not a magic bullet. Conclusions SRP alone reduces the bacterial load, inflammation and pocket depth and gains attachment. "Definitely know this one": antibiotics alone are not indicated in the treatment of periodontal disease, even though bacteria are the primary etiologic factor, and antimicrobials are not a first line of therapy. Combined with conventional therapy, they can add pocket reduction, less inflammation and attachment gain. Use them in selected cases (aggressive periodontitis, refractory periodontitis, areas of limited involvement in maintenance patients), and aim to remove the cause of attachment loss rather than treat the symptoms. His three references: the Lexi-Comp Drug Information Handbook for Dentistry (updated every year, with each drug's dental implications; one for the office), Epocrates (a free app, constantly updated, with every drug's dosing, mechanism and side effects; "everybody in this room should have this by the end of the day"), and the Little Dental Drug Booklet (about $20 and thin enough for the clinic, with common dental prescriptions written out to copy).
